name: Bragg's Law
statement: X-rays reflect strongly off crystal planes only at angles set by their spacing.
statementAccent: only at angles set by their spacing
meaning: When X-rays strike the parallel planes of atoms in a crystal, a strong reflection appears only at specific angles fixed by the plane spacing and the wavelength; at all other angles the scattered waves cancel. Because each strong-reflection angle maps to a plane spacing, measuring the angles reveals the crystal's internal geometry.
mechanism: Waves reflecting off successive planes travel different path lengths, and geometry makes the extra path equal to twice the plane spacing times the sine of the glancing angle. When that path difference is a whole number of wavelengths the reflected waves stay in phase and interfere constructively, giving a sharp Bragg peak; otherwise they cancel.

examples.text: Determining atomic and molecular structures from diffraction patterns, from simple salts to proteins — the technique behind, among much else, the discovery of DNA's double helix from its diffraction images.
Powder X-ray diffraction produces a set of plane spacings that act as a fingerprint, identifying an unknown mineral or crystalline phase.
The same condition governs neutrons and electrons whose wavelengths match atomic spacings, extending the method to probe crystal and magnetic structures.

variants.name: The Laue condition
variants.text: An equivalent, more general formulation in reciprocal space, from which Bragg's law can be derived — each Bragg reflection corresponds to a reciprocal-lattice vector.

variants.name: The dynamical theory of diffraction
variants.text: The fuller treatment for strong scatterers, perfect crystals, and multiple scattering, beyond the simple single-scattering picture Bragg's law assumes.

whyItMatters: It opened the atomic structure of matter to direct measurement, launching X-ray crystallography and, through it, much of modern chemistry, materials science, and structural biology. It is the condition that turns a diffraction pattern into a map of where atoms sit.

working.text: convert each strong-reflection angle into a plane spacing using the wavelength, building up the crystal geometry.

working.lead: Match the wavelength to the spacing
working.text: use radiation whose wavelength is comparable to atomic spacings — X-rays, neutrons, or electrons — since visible light is far too long.

working.lead: Look beyond peak positions for intensities
working.text: remember the law gives where peaks fall, not how strong they are; intensities need the structure factor and the arrangement within the unit cell.

limits: Bragg's law is an idealised picture, treating diffraction as mirror-like reflection off imaginary planes when real scattering is by discrete atoms; the planes are a geometric convenience. It gives peak positions but not intensities, which depend on the atomic arrangement within the unit cell. It belongs to the simpler kinematic theory of weak single scattering; the fuller dynamical theory is needed for strong scatterers, perfect crystals, and multiple scattering, notably in electron diffraction. It also assumes large periodic crystals and a wavelength comparable to the spacing.
misreadings: The 'reflection' is a heuristic, not literal — atoms scatter, and the planes are a device — and the law fixes only the angles of peaks, saying nothing about their intensities. It is exact within the kinematic, large-crystal idealisation, and gives way to the dynamical theory when scattering is strong.
origin: Formulated by William Lawrence Bragg with his father William Henry Bragg in 1912–1913; they shared the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics for analysing crystal structure with X-rays, and the younger Bragg remains the youngest physics laureate.
namedAfter: William Lawrence Bragg and William Henry Bragg
